section.title: Send Out Your Light and Truth
section.sectionRationale: The conclusion of the single poem begun in Psalm 42, sharing its identical closing refrain. Here the downcast soul turns from remembered anguish to active petition, asking God to vindicate him and to send out light and truth to lead him home to the altar of God, his greatest joy.
section.thesis: Still opposed by an ungodly nation and deceitful men, the psalmist asks God to vindicate him and to send out His light and truth to guide him back to the altar, resolving the whole poem's downcast refrain in the settled hope that he will yet praise his Savior and God.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the plea for vindication and for God's light and truth to lead the way home, verses 1-4; and the closing refrain of hope, verse 5, identical to Psalm 42:11, resolving the shared poem.

units.label: Send out Your light and Your truth

verses.text:
{{shaphat|Vindicate}} me, O God, and plead my case against an ungodly nation; 
deliver me from deceitful and unjust men.
For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy's oppression?
Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain, and to the place where You dwell.
Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God.
Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.

shaphat.gloss: To judge, vindicate, or plead a legal case. The psalmist asks God to act as his advocate and judge, formally clearing his name and pleading his cause against those who wrong him, language of the law court applied to personal distress.

basic.context: Continuing straight on from Psalm 42 without a separate heading in the Hebrew manuscripts, this psalm moves the same downcast soul from remembered anguish into active petition. The psalmist asks God to vindicate him against an ungodly nation and deceitful men, and prays that God's own light and truth would go out ahead of him like guides, leading him back to the altar, his greatest joy, where he will again praise with the harp.
basic.hermeneutics: Read as the conclusion of one continuous prayer with Psalm 42, this psalm shows lament properly resolving not in the removal of every circumstance but in renewed petition and a settled resolve to praise, the same refrain now bringing the whole poem to its close.
basic.originalLanguages: The opening plea, shaphat, vindicate, is law-court language, asking God to act as judge and advocate, pleading the psalmist's case formally rather than merely offering private comfort. Light and truth are personified, sent out like messengers or guides to lead the way home.
basic.typology: The plea to be vindicated against unjust accusers and led by God's own light and truth to His dwelling place anticipates Christ, who was Himself unjustly accused yet vindicated by God in the resurrection, and who is Himself called the light of the world, John 8:12, and the way, the truth, and the life, John 14:6, leading His people to God's presence.
basic.christ: The psalmist prays that God would send out light and truth to lead him to the altar of God. Jesus declares Himself to be exactly this: 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6. What the psalmist asked God to send, light and truth as guides home, God sent fully and finally in the person of His Son, who also, like this psalmist, was unjustly accused yet vindicated by God through the resurrection.
basic.god: God is shown as both refuge and judge, the one to whom the wronged bring their case for vindication, and the one whose own light and truth, sent out like living guides, alone can lead the soul home to worship.
basic.crossReferences: John 8:12 records Jesus declaring Himself the light of the world. John 14:6 records Jesus declaring Himself the way, the truth, and the life, leading to the Father. Romans 8:33-34 shows God as the one who vindicates and justifies His people against every accusation.
basic.oneStory: The psalmist's plea for vindication and for God's light and truth to lead him home to worship anticipates Christ, who is Himself the light and the truth, unjustly accused yet vindicated by the Father, now leading all who trust Him to the true dwelling place of God's presence.

context.literary:
Psalm 43 is the third stanza of the poem that began at 42:1 and the only one that speaks mostly in commands. Where the earlier stanzas described thirst and flood, this one is a string of imperatives: 'Vindicate me', 'plead my case', 'deliver me', 'Send out', 'let them lead me'. The poet has moved from lament to petition, and the change is marked by a sudden legal tone in verse 1 and a sudden geography in verse 3, which names the holy mountain and the dwelling place.

The five verses fall into a simple ladder. Verses 1 and 2 are the low step: enemies, injustice, and the complaint 'Why have You rejected me?' Verses 3 and 4 climb: God's light and truth go out, lead the poet up to the mountain, and bring him to the altar, where the voice of praise is finally heard with the harp. Verse 5 closes the ladder with the refrain, so the last word of the whole poem returns to self-address. The poem does not end on the altar. It ends on a man who is still speaking to his own soul, and who has learned to expect praise before he has arrived at the place of praise.

There is also a link back to the previous stanza. The complaint of verse 2, 'Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy's oppression?', repeats 42:9 word for word. That repetition works as a hinge between the two chapters and is one of the strongest reasons scholars read them as a unit. The 'why' questions of 42:9 and 43:2 mirror the 'why' of the refrain, so the poem contains three different kinds of question: to the soul, to God, and about the enemy.

The verbs of movement give the psalm its shape. Light and truth are sent out, they lead, they bring; the poet then goes, and finally praises. Everything is in motion toward the altar.
context.historical:
Psalm 43 has no heading of its own, and several Hebrew manuscripts join it to Psalm 42, as the BSB footnote on 42 records. Its historical setting is therefore that of Psalm 42: a Levite of the Korahite guild, far from Jerusalem and mocked by those who doubt his God. What Psalm 43 adds is the legal language of a man who believes he has been wronged by other people. The 'ungodly nation' and the 'deceitful and unjust men' of verse 1 are not only sceptics who taunt but people who act against him.

The world in which this prayer was prayed treated disputes as cases before a judge. In Israel, a wronged person could bring his cause to the elders at the gate, and where human courts failed, appeal was made to God as the last judge, 1 Samuel 24:15. The poet is doing that here, and the verb 'plead my case' is the language of the courtroom. The fact that he must appeal to God shows that no earthly court is open to him. He is either abroad or powerless.

The places named in the psalm are the sanctuary places. The 'holy mountain' is Zion, the temple hill, Psalm 2:6. The 'place where You dwell' uses the plural word for dwellings in the Hebrew, the same word that appears in Psalm 84:1 for the Lord's dwelling place. The 'altar of God' points to the daily sacrifices that the poet cannot now attend, and the 'harp' is the instrument of the temple guilds, 1 Chronicles 25:1. The singer wants to return, not only to a place, but to a job: he wants to lead praise again.

Whoever the enemy was, the first hearers would have understood the request. A people exiled, or a Levite far away, needed a vindication that would put them back in worship.
context.canonical:
Psalm 43 completes what Psalm 42 began, and it gave the church one of its most used prayers. The Latin opening, 'Judica me, Deus', was the psalm said at the foot of the altar at the start of the Mass in the Western church. The Reformation tradition has valued the psalm for a different reason, its plain grammar of hope in the middle of injustice.

Within the Psalter, the pairing of light and truth with a journey to God's house appears again. Psalm 27:1 declares, 'The LORD is my light and my salvation', and asks to dwell in His house; Psalm 57:3 says, 'God sends forth His loving devotion and His truth'. The idea that God sends out His attributes like servants ahead of a traveller is a rare and vivid one. Psalm 89:14 places 'loving devotion and faithfulness' before God's face, so the goodness of God is imagined as a retinue.

The psalm looks forward in two ways. The first is the theme of a vindicating God, taken up in Romans 8:33, 'It is God who justifies'. The second is the identity of the light and truth. John's Gospel says of the Word made flesh that He was 'full of grace and truth', John 1:14, and Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world', John 8:12, and 'I am the way and the truth and the life', John 14:6. The psalm's prayer is answered by a person who is both.

The final image of the poem, the altar and the harp, is taken up in the book of Revelation, where the redeemed sing before the throne with harps, Revelation 15:2. The poet's private return becomes the church's public arrival.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet intends the community to hear a prayer that asks for the right things in the right order. He does not begin with what he wants from his enemies. He begins with what he wants from God, a verdict, and only then with what he wants for himself, a road. The road is not merely out of trouble but toward worship: 'Then I will go to the altar of God'. The request for vindication is justified by the purpose it serves, that the singer may sing.

He also wants hearers to see that God is a fit object of appeal. The hinge of verse 2, 'You are the God of my refuge', is placed immediately beside 'Why have You rejected me?' The pair of statements is deliberate, and it teaches Israel to hold complaint and confidence together. The poet trusts the very God he questions.

The refrain in verse 5 is the third and last, and its effect on the choir is to make the sung prayer end with the same command it started with. That would have taught the hearers that resolution in the life of faith often looks less like solved circumstances and more like a renewed decision to hope. The psalm tells them to sing and to wait, and to expect that God will send His light and truth for the journey.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The prayer for vindication is a description of one man's plea, not a licence for believers to ask for the ruin of enemies. It is worth noticing that the poet asks God to do the judging and does not take the matter into his own hands. That is the instructive part. Christians are told in Romans 12:19 to leave room for God's wrath, and this psalm shows what leaving room looks like: bringing the case to God and asking Him to rule.

The request that light and truth would 'lead me' to the holy mountain is likewise a prayer, not a promise that a particular believer will be brought to a particular place. The text does not say how God answers in every case. What it does establish is the shape of a good request: it asks for guidance, for the presence of God, and for the ability to worship. A modern reader can pray this way without claiming that every wish will be granted in the poet's terms.

Finally, the altar and the harp describe the worship of the time. The New Testament does not command believers to seek an altar in Jerusalem. It teaches that access to God comes through Christ, Hebrews 10:19-22, and that praise is offered by the church wherever it gathers. The principle the psalm gives, that God Himself is the joy to which the pilgrim goes, remains, while the location has changed.

debates.question: Are Psalms 42 and 43 one poem or two?

views.label: One poem in three stanzas
views.case: Psalm 43 has no heading, unlike the psalms around it. The refrain appears three times across the two chapters, and 43:2 repeats 42:9 almost exactly. Several Hebrew manuscripts join them, as the BSB footnote records, and the shape of the poem is more complete when 43 is read as its ending.

views.label: Two related psalms
views.case: The Hebrew Bible as received divides them, and the tone of 43 is different: petition and legal appeal rather than remembering. Some interpreters think 43 was composed as a companion or a response, added to the collection because of the shared refrain.

debates.bearing: The unity view better explains the repeated refrain and the missing heading. Either way, the poem is best heard as one movement from thirst to petition to settled hope.

debates.question: Who is the 'ungodly nation' of verse 1?

views.label: A foreign people holding the psalmist
views.case: The Hebrew for nation is the word normally used of Gentiles, and the psalmist's location far from Zion suggests he is among foreigners who mock his God, as in 42:3. The word rendered 'ungodly' means something like 'lacking in covenant loyalty', which fits a nation that has no place for the Lord.

views.label: Israelites who oppress him
views.case: The phrase could also point to a faction within Israel. The prophets sometimes call Israel a nation that has failed in loyalty, and the 'deceitful and unjust men' of the same verse might be local persecutors.

views.label: An open category
views.case: The psalm gives no specifics, and the poetry is written so that any worshipper facing unjust opposition can pray it.

debates.bearing: The text does not tell us, and the prayer does not need to know. What matters is that the appeal is to a judge who can tell the difference between the loyal and the disloyal.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening plea uses shaphat, which is the ordinary word for judging, in an imperative, and it is coupled with rib, 'plead my case'. The second verb is the language of a lawsuit. Elsewhere David says to Saul that the Lord will judge between them and plead his cause, 1 Samuel 24:15, and Micah 7:9 has a penitent Israel say that God will argue her case and execute justice for her. The psalmist takes the courtroom word and puts God in the roles of judge and advocate, which is the unusual and daring part.

The description of the opponents is careful. The nation is one that is not chasid, that is, not marked by chesed, the loyal love that binds a covenant people. The BSB renders it 'ungodly', but the sense is closer to 'without covenant loyalty'. The deceitful and unjust men are two more descriptions of persons whose speech and conduct are false. The poet lines up the opposition in terms of character rather than only of power.

The word for refuge in verse 2, ma'oz, is a stronghold, a fortified place, so the poet calls God the God of his fortress. The same verse's 'rejected' is zanach, the verb that also appears in Psalm 44:9 and 44:23 and again in Psalm 74:1, the protests of the people who cannot understand why God has left them. The poet's private word becomes a national one in the psalms that follow.

Verse 3 gives the most notable image. 'Light' and 'truth' are named in the Hebrew as things God sends, and the verbs 'let them lead me' and 'let them bring me' are imperatives in the third person, treating the attributes as messengers. The parallel in Psalm 57:3 is that God 'sends forth His loving devotion and His truth', where the verb is the same, shalach. The word for truth, emet, is the word for reliability, something that holds. Light and reliability are thus God's guides on a dark road.

The last cluster in verse 4 is 'to God, my greatest joy'. The Hebrew is closer to 'to God, the gladness of my rejoicing', a stacking of two joy words. It shows that the joy is God Himself and not the sacrifices.

typology.type: The plea for vindication before an unjust court, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The righteous man who asks God to plead his case and to judge between him and a treacherous people finds his greatest counterpart in Jesus, who stood before the council and Pilate, accused by false witnesses, Matthew 26:59-60. Christ did not open His mouth in His own defence but 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly', 1 Peter 2:23. The vindication the psalmist sought comes in the resurrection, which declares Christ to be the Son of God, Romans 1:4. Believers share in it, because 'Who is there to condemn us? For Christ Jesus, who died', Romans 8:34. The type is limited in that the psalmist asks for judgment on enemies, while Christ prays for their forgiveness, Luke 23:34.

typology.type: Light and truth sent out to lead, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: God sends His light and truth like two guides. In the fullness of time He sends His Son, who says, 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness', John 8:12, and 'I am the way and the truth and the life', John 14:6. John says that the Word who made His dwelling among us was 'full of grace and truth', John 1:14. The psalm's two messengers become one person. The type has its limits, since the psalmist was asking for guidance and not for an incarnation, and the fulfilment far exceeds the request; the guide does not merely lead to the mountain but is Himself the way.

typology.type: The journey to the altar and the holy mountain, verses 3 and 4
typology.fulfillment: The pilgrim's road to Zion and the altar is a type of the believer's approach to God. Hebrews teaches that Christ's sacrifice opened a new and living way, so believers may enter the holy place with confidence, Hebrews 10:19-22, and that they have come 'to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God', Hebrews 12:22. The altar where the poet will bring his praise is replaced by the cross, on which Christ offered Himself once for all, and the people themselves become a house of praise, Hebrews 13:15. The type falls short because the psalm could only point to a place; the fulfilment is a person and a people.

study.christ:
The centre of the psalm's Christian reading is verse 3: 'Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me.' Nowhere else in the Psalter is the guidance of God so nearly personified, and the New Testament claims both terms for Jesus. In the Gospel of John, light is the great symbol of the Son's mission. 'I am the light of the world', He says, and the one who follows Him 'will have the light of life', John 8:12. At the opening of the Gospel the Word is the light that shines in the darkness, and later He is 'full of grace and truth', John 1:14. In John 14:6 He says, 'I am the way and the truth and the life.' The psalmist prays for guides that will lead him to the holy mountain; the Gospel says that the guide has come and that He is Himself the way there.

The legal frame of the psalm also finds its fulfilment in Christ. The poet asks God to vindicate him against unjust men. Jesus was the one who stood in front of unjust men and was condemned, yet 1 Peter 2:23 says that He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. The Father's answer is the resurrection. Romans 1:4 says He was declared the Son of God with power by the resurrection from the dead, and 1 Timothy 3:16 says He was vindicated in the Spirit. Because He was vindicated, His people are, Romans 8:33-34. This means that the plea of Psalm 43 is answered for believers not by a change in circumstances but by a verdict.

The psalm also leads to Christ in its goal. The poet wants to reach the altar, and the God of his greatest joy. Christ is the sacrifice and the priest, and He is the temple in whom God dwells, John 2:19-21. Through Him the way into God's presence is open, Hebrews 10:19-20. The poem ends with a promise that praise will come, and in the New Testament praise comes through Him, Hebrews 13:15.

Caution is needed. The psalm does not predict Jesus by name, and its language of unjust men and holy mountain belongs first to its own world. The link is the pattern and the vocabulary: a righteous man in need of a guide and a judge, and a God who sends both. The Christian claim is that God sent both in one person.
study.god:
The first truth about God in this psalm is that He is judge. The poet does not lay out a case for his enemies' guilt in his own strength; he asks God to hear it. This is a picture of a God who cares about right and wrong, who is not indifferent to injustice, and who can be trusted to settle it. The doctrine here is that God is the final court, and that those who have no earthly hearing are never without one.

The second truth is that God is refuge. Verse 2 links the courtroom and the stronghold. The one who judges is also the one who shelters. A judge can seem remote and a stronghold can seem merely a wall, but the psalm gives both titles to one person.

Third, the psalm shows God as one who sends. Light and truth go out from Him and lead. This is a rich picture of divine guidance. God does not merely give a map; He sends His own reliability and brightness to walk with the traveller. The attributes are not abstractions in the psalmist's mind but agents, and the effect is to make God present on the road. In the context of exile that is a bold claim: the God whose house is far away sends His character across the distance.

Fourth, God is the goal. The poet wants to reach the altar, but it is 'God, my greatest joy' to whom the altar leads. He does not seek the gift of the temple but the giver. That gives worship its centre: the joy of the people of God is God Himself.

The psalm also holds a tension without resolving it. The God of refuge is asked why He has rejected. The psalm does not explain the rejection, and it does not deny the refuge. It sets both in front of God and leaves them there. Worship, in this poem, is being honest about the tension and refusing to abandon either side.

For worship, the psalm gives a model of prayer that is bold, ordered and hopeful: ask for justice, ask for a road, and promise praise. It ends with a soul instructed to hope. A congregation praying this psalm is learning that God is worth waiting for.

crossReferences.note: The complaint 'Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy's oppression?' appears here nearly word for word and reappears in 43:2. The repetition welds the two chapters into one poem and shows the same question being carried from lament into petition.

David declares that the Lord is his light and his salvation. It gives the background for Psalm 43:3, where light is something God sends. In Psalm 27 the same person also longs to dwell in the Lord's house, so the two psalms share the idea that God's light leads to His presence.

God 'sends forth His loving devotion and His truth', as He is asked to send light and truth in 43:3. The parallel shows that in the Psalter God's attributes can be pictured as messengers who go ahead of His people and carry them through danger.

The Korahite pilgrim psalm exclaims, 'How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of Hosts!' It uses the same vocabulary of God's dwelling as Psalm 43:3 and expresses the same wish to reach the sanctuary. The two psalms belong to one guild and one hope.

Israel, repenting under discipline, says that God will plead her case and execute justice for her, and bring her out into the light. It shares the legal idea of Psalm 43:1 and the promise of light, and it shows the same trust in God as advocate even when the sufferer is not blameless.

Paul asks who can bring a charge against God's elect and answers that God justifies and Christ intercedes. It is the New Testament answer to the psalmist's plea: the vindication asked for is given in Christ, and it does not depend on any change in the enemy.

Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world.' The psalmist prays for light to lead him; here the light stands in person and promises that those who follow Him will not walk in darkness. It is the clearest link between the psalm's request and the Gospel's claim.

Jesus is the way, the truth and the life. The two guides of Psalm 43:3, light and truth, are gathered in a single speaker, and the destination the psalm names, the place where God dwells, is described here as the Father, to whom no one comes except through Him.

Believers may enter the holy place by the blood of Jesus, through a new and living way. It answers the psalmist's wish to be brought to the altar and the place where God dwells, showing that the road he prayed for has been opened by Christ.

The redeemed stand beside the sea holding harps from God. The harp of Psalm 43:4, promised as the sound of arrival at the altar, becomes the instrument of the whole company of the saved in the final worship.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 43 sits in the story of a people who have lost the place where God met them and who are learning to pray their way back. Its opening is the courtroom, and the courtroom has a long history in Scripture. In Genesis 3, God is the judge who calls Adam and Eve to account and then sends them out of the garden. The rest of the Old Testament is full of injustice that the faithful bring to Him: Abel's blood cries from the ground, Genesis 4:10; Israel groans under Pharaoh, Exodus 2:23-24; the prophets protest against oppression. Psalm 43 belongs to that stream of appeal to the Judge of all the earth, Genesis 18:25.

Its second movement is the road. The Bible is a story of journeys toward the presence of God: from Eden outward, from Egypt to Sinai, from exile to Zion. The psalm asks for light and truth to lead the way, and elsewhere in the Bible God does give guides, the pillar of cloud and fire, the law, the prophets, and finally the Son. In Jesus the light and truth of God arrive in person, and the road to the mountain and the altar is opened by His death, Hebrews 10:19-20.

The psalm ends with a promise of praise. That too runs through the story. The exiles return and sing, Psalm 126:1-3, and the people of God are commissioned to declare His praises, 1 Peter 2:9. The poet's vow to praise with the harp is fulfilled beyond his imagining when the redeemed stand before the throne, Revelation 15:2 and 5:8-9.

In the new creation the poem's questions are settled. The nations that taunted have no power, the deceitful are outside the city, Revelation 22:15, and God's dwelling is with man, Revelation 21:3. The light is no longer sent along a road, because the city has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb, Revelation 21:23. The soul that was commanded to hope now sees the object of its hope, and the refrain gives way to sight.

sermon.title: I Will Go to God, My Exceeding Joy
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly on Psalm 43, tracing how the psalmist moves from vindication and God's sent-out light and truth toward the settled resolve to go to God Himself as his exceeding joy, a pattern for moving from downcast lament to renewed worship.

quiz.q: What legal language does the psalmist use to open his plea in verse 1?

options.text: He asks God to vindicate him, using courtroom language of judging and pleading a case.
options.note: Shaphat pictures God acting as judge and advocate, formally clearing the psalmist's name.

options.text: He asks God to forget the whole matter entirely.
options.note: The plea is for active vindication and a pleaded case, not for the matter to simply be forgotten.

options.text: He asks his human accusers to judge him fairly.
options.note: The plea is addressed to God, not to the accusers themselves, asking God to plead his case against them.

options.text: He asks for a delay in any judgment.
options.note: The plea is for active, prompt vindication, not for delaying judgment.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask God to send out in verse 3?

options.text: His light and His truth, to lead him to God's holy mountain and dwelling place.
options.note: These are personified as guides sent ahead, an image Jesus fulfills directly in John 8:12 and John 14:6.

options.text: An army to defeat his enemies.
options.note: The specific request is for light and truth as guides, not military force.

options.text: Wealth to compensate for his losses.
options.note: The request concerns guidance home to worship, not material compensation.

options.text: A message of comfort to his friends.
options.note: The request is for personal guidance to God's presence, not a message directed at friends.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist say he will do once he reaches the altar of God, verse 4?

options.text: Praise God with the harp, calling Him his greatest joy.
options.note: Arrival at the altar is tied directly to renewed, joyful, musical praise.

options.text: Offer a formal complaint against his accusers.
options.note: At the altar the response described is praise and joy, not further complaint.

options.text: Remain silent out of exhaustion.
options.note: The text explicitly describes active praise with the harp, not silence.

options.text: Ask for permission to leave again immediately.
options.note: The tone describes God as his greatest joy at the altar, the opposite of wanting to leave immediately.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's closing refrain in verse 5 relate to Psalm 42?

options.text: It is word for word identical to the refrain in Psalm 42:11, showing the two psalms form one continuous poem.
options.note: This shared refrain, appearing in 42:5, 42:11, and 43:5, is strong evidence the two psalms were composed as a unified prayer.

options.text: It directly contradicts everything said in Psalm 42.
options.note: The refrain is identical, not contradictory, showing continuity rather than contradiction.

options.text: It introduces an entirely new and unrelated theme.
options.note: The refrain repeats the same words used in Psalm 42, rather than introducing something new.

options.text: It is found nowhere else in the Psalter.
options.note: While the refrain is distinctive to this shared poem, the point is that it recurs identically three times within Psalms 42-43, not that it appears nowhere else at all within these two psalms.

quiz.q: How does Jesus take up this psalm's image of light and truth sent to guide the way?

options.text: He declares Himself both the light of the world, John 8:12, and the way, the truth, and the life, John 14:6.
options.note: Jesus applies both images from this psalm directly to Himself as the one who leads people to the Father.

options.text: He rejects any association with light or truth in His teaching.
options.note: Jesus explicitly and repeatedly claims both titles for Himself in John's Gospel.

options.text: He applies the image only to the Holy Spirit, never to Himself.
options.note: While the Spirit is also called the Spirit of truth, John 14:6 and John 8:12 have Jesus applying these titles directly to Himself.

options.text: He applies the image only to John the Baptist.
options.note: John the Baptist testified to the light, John 1:8, but Jesus explicitly claims the title of light and truth for Himself.

questions: The psalmist asks God to vindicate him against unjust accusers rather than defending himself. Where do you need to entrust your reputation or vindication to God rather than fighting for it yourself?
The psalmist prays for God's light and truth to be sent out ahead of him like guides. What decision or season of confusion in your life right now needs God's light and truth to lead the way?

Verse 4 calls God 'my greatest joy.' Would you honestly describe God, rather than any other person, achievement, or comfort, as your greatest joy right now? What would need to change for that to be true?

This psalm and Psalm 42 share the same refrain, showing lament resolving not by denying pain but by repeated, active choice to hope. What refrain of truth do you need to preach to your own soul repeatedly this week?
Jesus declares Himself both the light and the truth this psalmist longed for. How does praying this psalm differently, knowing Christ Himself is the answer to its plea, change how you pray it?

translationNotes.note: Vindicate renders shaphat, courtroom language for judging or pleading a legal case, asking God to act as advocate and judge on the psalmist's behalf.
Light and truth are personified as messengers or guides sent out ahead of the psalmist, an image Jesus later applies directly to Himself in John 8:12 and John 14:6.
This refrain is identical to Psalm 42:11, strong evidence that Psalms 42 and 43 were originally composed as one continuous poem.
